source.title: Hierarchical Weight Averaging for Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Xiao-Zhe Gu; Zixun Zhang; Yuncheng Jiang; Tao Luo; Rui-Mao Zhang; Shu-Guang Cui; Zhuguo Li

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is present, though some mathematical notation and figure contents are garbled or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: Tests online and offline weight averaging on several image datasets and architectures, reporting effects on test accuracy and selected training/test accuracy comparisons; these WA findings are not directly covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-accuracy comparisons for HWA, SWA, and other methods, plus selected training/test accuracy trajectories. These results bear on generalization but do not test a listed version's specific claim. Cited findings from prior work are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates weight-averaging methods and uses a flat-minima explanation for their performance. Its results do not test V1–V8. In particular, loss-landscape projections and SAM accuracy comparisons do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that combining online and offline averaging improves convergence and generalization relative to either alone, and explain the improvements through loss-landscape geometry. The flat-side account is an explanatory interpretation; their account of restarts causing memorized hard examples to be forgotten is explicitly speculative.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates weight averaging methods, not the random-label memorization, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or memorized-example interventions in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that offline SWA performance is sensitive to its sampling-stage learning rate; Table II also shows SWA below baseline for ResNet110 on CIFAR100. Slide-window length affects test accuracy differently across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: HWA improves reported test accuracy over the conventional baseline across the extracted CIFAR and ImageNet conditions. SWA improves most extracted conditions but reduces ResNet110 CIFAR100 accuracy from 73.21 to 71.57.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical weight averaging can improve image-classification accuracy; offline averaging benefits depend on the architecture and sampling recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: For ResNet20 on CIFAR100, the averaged endpoint has lower training accuracy and higher test accuracy than the individual endpoint in Figure 9.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight averaging can improve held-out accuracy while reducing training accuracy within a connected low-loss region.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The paper's evidence concerns image-classification benchmarks and weight-averaging comparisons, not the listed versions' interventions. Uncertainty estimates are not reported for the extracted table values. Some mechanistic explanations rely on plotted loss-surface projections, and the paper itself describes its account of restart effects as a possible explanation.
record.rows_left_out: Table II includes additional comparator methods (CA, RePr, FG, SAM) for the same architectures and datasets; these were left out to prioritize HWA and SWA comparisons. Table V–VII include further dataset and architecture accuracy results, Table III reports module ablations, and Table IV varies the number of parallel models; these additional weight-averaging outcomes are not separately extracted because they do not map to a listed version and the result set is extensive.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level random-label test accuracy compared with natural-label generalization under matched architectures and recipes.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, weight-decay changes, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that reduce large-batch penalties. Varying the number of parallel HWA models does not isolate batch size.
Dropout addition, removal, strength, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Influence-defined memorization and retraining after removing highly memorized versus random examples. The proposed forgetting explanation supplies no such experiment.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply because no listed version is tested. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, even where a weight-averaging accuracy improvement or decline is clear. CIFAR baselines use stepwise learning-rate decay, whereas HWA uses cosine decay by default, so baseline comparisons also change the schedule.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps past interpolation and test error as width changes.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning regimes.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to large batches.
Dropout addition/removal and its effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
